title: Two tides a day
teaches: Why the Moon raises two bulges, the Sun's share, and spring and neap tides
summary: **The tide keeps the Moon's time.** Most coasts have two high tides about 12 hours 25 minutes apart, coming about 50 minutes later each day.
**Tides come from a difference in pull.** The Moon pulls the near side of the Earth harder than its centre and the far side less, and what is left over stretches the ocean.
**So there are two bulges.** One lies under the Moon and one on the opposite side, and each place is carried through both as the Earth turns.
**The push that matters is sideways.** Straight up, the tide-raising force is far too weak to lift water; along the surface nothing resists it, and it slides the ocean into the bulges.
**The Sun raises a tide a bit under half the Moon's.** Its pull is 180 times stronger, but it is so far away that its pull hardly changes across the Earth.
**Spring tides come at new and full moon.** The Sun's and Moon's bulges line up and add; at the quarter moons they lie across each other and give the smaller neap tides.
**The real tide is bigger and later than this picture.** Seattle's range is several times the half metre the bulges predict, and its two daily tides are unequal: lessons 9 and 10 take up why.

parts.title: A tide on the far side

blocks.text: Anyone who lives by the sea learns the tide's rhythm. The water rises for about six hours to **high water** (high tide), falls for about six to **low water**, and the whole pattern comes about fifty minutes later each day, keeping time with the Moon rather than the Sun. Writers in the ancient world already tied the tide to the Moon. How the Moon did it stayed a puzzle for two thousand years. In 1609 Johannes Kepler suggested that the Moon draws the water toward it, much as a magnet draws iron, and Galileo scoffed at the idea; Isaac Newton gave the answer in 1687, in the *Principia*, the book in which he set out his law of gravity.

Kepler was partly right: the Moon's gravity does raise the tide. But his picture fails a simple test. If the Moon only pulled the water toward it, the sea would heap up on the side of the Earth facing the Moon, and every coast would have one high tide a day, when the Moon was overhead. Instead most coasts have two, about twelve and a half hours apart, and the second comes when the Moon is on the opposite side of the Earth, out of sight. Something raises the water on the side facing away from the Moon. This is still the common misconception about tides, and the far bulge is what Newton explained.

Gravity weakens with distance: twice as far away, a pull is a quarter as strong. The Moon is about 384,000 km away, sixty times the Earth's radius of 6,400 km. So the side of the Earth facing the Moon is a sixtieth closer to it than the Earth's centre is, and the far side a sixtieth farther. Because the pull goes with one over the distance squared, a sixtieth closer makes it about two sixtieths stronger: the near side is pulled about 3% harder than the centre, and the far side about 3% less.

The Earth and the Moon orbit a shared balance point, which lies inside the Earth, about 4,700 km from its centre. An orbit is a fall that never lands: the Earth is falling toward the Moon all the time while moving sideways fast enough to keep missing. What drives that fall is the Moon's pull at the Earth's centre, and every rock and every drop of water moves along with it. So the Moon's pull at a place can do only one thing besides carry it along with the Earth: whatever is left when the pull at the centre is taken away. That leftover is the **tide-raising force**. With what the last paragraph says about the near and far sides, the figure's question can be worked out before stepping through.

blocks.caption: The Moon's pull at twelve points round the Earth (purple arrows), seen from above the North Pole with the Moon far off to the right. Three buttons step from the pull itself, to the pull with the centre's pull taken away (black arrows), to what is left. The water's bulges are drawn hugely exaggerated.
blocks.task: Guess, then step through to what is left

blocks.text: On the near side the Moon pulls a little harder than at the centre, so the water there is pulled toward the Moon, away from the Earth's centre. On the far side the Moon pulls a little less than at the centre: the Earth falls toward the Moon slightly faster than that water does, and the water lags behind, which also takes it away from the Earth's centre. Round the middle, where the Moon is on the horizon, the points are about as far from the Moon as the centre is, so the pulls there are nearly the same size as the centre's. But they all aim at the Moon, so they slant in very slightly toward the line through the Earth's middle, while the centre's pull runs straight along it. Take away the centre's pull and that slight slant is what is left: a small push inward, about half the size of the outward pull at the bulges. The ocean is stretched into two bulges, one under the Moon and one on the opposite side.[^centrifugal]

**Estimate.** Write g for the pull of the Earth's own gravity at its surface. The Moon's whole pull on the Earth is about three millionths of g, and the tide-raising force is the small difference between two such pulls: at its strongest, under the Moon, about a nine-millionth of g. It makes a 70 kg person lighter by about the weight of 8 milligrams, less than a grain of rice. Straight up, it could never lift the sea against gravity. What moves the ocean is its sideways part along the surface, called the **tractive force**. Nothing resists that: the ocean sits on the Earth like water in a dish, and a slight sideways push on every drop across a whole ocean slides the water toward the points under and opposite the Moon.[^tractive]

The bulges stay lined up with the Moon while the Earth turns beneath them. A place on the coast is carried through one bulge, then a low, then the other bulge, then a second low: two high tides and two low tides each time round.

blocks.caption: The Earth turns under the two bulges, carrying a place (black dot) through high, low, high and low water. A picture of the bulges alone, drawn hugely exaggerated; the real tide at any coast arrives later and in its own shape.

blocks.text: Meanwhile the Moon moves on along its orbit, about 13 degrees a day in the same direction as the Earth turns. After one full turn of the Earth a place has to turn a little farther to catch the Moon up, and it takes 24 hours and 50 minutes to come back under it. So the high tides come about 12 hours 25 minutes apart, and fifty minutes later each day.

If the ocean could keep up with the Moon, the height of its bulges would be easy to estimate. The water's surface tilts until gravity, pulling down the slope, balances the tractive force pushing up it. The tractive force is at most about a twelve-millionth of g, so the surface can slope by at most about one part in twelve million, and on average about two thirds of that over the 10,000 km from the point under the Moon to the middle of a low. Ten thousand kilometres at that slope is a rise of about half a metre. That is the **range**, the drop from the top of a bulge to the bottom of a low, in what is called the **equilibrium tide**: the tide the ocean would have if it had time to settle into the shape the forces ask for. Hold on to that half metre.

The Sun raises a tide in the same way. Its pull on the Earth is about 180 times the Moon's: it is what holds the Earth in its orbit. By that measure the Sun ought to swamp the Moon's tide. It doesn't, because a tide comes from the difference in pull across the Earth, and the Sun is about 390 times farther away than the Moon.

Work it the same way as for the Moon. The Earth's near side is a sixtieth of the way closer to the Moon, which made the Moon's pull there about 3.3% stronger than at the centre. For the Sun, 390 times as far away, the near side is only about one 23,000th of the way closer, so the Sun's pull there is only about 0.0085% stronger than at the centre. The Sun's tide-raising force is 0.0085% of a pull 180 times the Moon's, against 3.3% of the Moon's own: 180 × 0.0085 is about 1.5, and 1.5 is a bit under half of 3.3. The farther away a body is, the less its pull changes across the Earth, on top of the pull itself being weaker, which is why tides fall off with the cube of distance.[^cube]

blocks.caption: The pulls of the Sun and Moon on the Earth, and their tide-raising forces, in millionths of g (µg, where g is the pull of the Earth's own gravity). The scale is a ratio scale: each step along it is ten times the last, so very different numbers fit on one chart. The Sun pulls far harder; the Moon raises the bigger tide.

options.title: Pull, and the difference across the Earth

items.label: The Sun's pull on the Earth
The Moon's pull on the Earth

blocks.text: So the Earth carries two pairs of bulges: the Moon's, and the Sun's, a bit under half as tall. Each pair points along a line through the Earth: the Moon's toward the Moon and directly away from it, the Sun's toward the Sun and directly away. The Moon goes round the Earth once a month, 29.5 days from one new moon to the next, so the angle between the two lines goes round too. At new moon the Moon lies between the Earth and the Sun, at full moon on the far side of the Earth from the Sun, and at the first and last quarters it is at right angles to the Sun. (Why that gives the Moon's phases is in the Astronomy course.) With that, the figure's question can be worked out before the month is played through.

blocks.caption: A month of the Moon's bulge (purple, dashed), the Sun's (gold, dashed) and their sum (blue), seen from above the North Pole with the Sun far off to the left. The Play button runs the month; the slider moves through it by hand. Below, the tide they raise at one place on the equator, in units of the Moon's tide alone. The equilibrium tide, a model; the real ocean answers later and unequally.
blocks.task: Guess, then play the month through

blocks.text: At new moon and at full moon the two lines are the same line, and the bulges add: the highs are higher and the lows lower. These are **spring tides**, with a range about 1.46 times the Moon's own in this picture (1 plus the Sun's 0.46).[^spring] At the first and last quarter moons the Sun's bulges lie across the Moon's and fill in its lows, and the range drops to about 0.54 of the Moon's own (1 less 0.46): the **neap tides**. Springs and neaps take turns, about 7.4 days apart, so springs come round every two weeks.

**Out in the field.** NOAA's tide predictions for Seattle (station 9447130) are free online and take a few minutes to read. Look up the ranges for the days around a full or new moon, and for the days around a quarter moon a week later. The biggest ranges do cluster near new and full moon. The pattern is untidier than the figure: some springs are much bigger than others,[^perigee] the biggest ranges come a day or two after the new or full moon, not on it, and the two tides on the same day are often far from equal.

Newton's picture explains the forcing: why there are two tides a day, why they come fifty minutes later each day, and why their range swells and shrinks over two weeks. It does not explain the tide at Seattle.

It gets the size wrong. Seattle's two high tides each day are usually of different heights, and so are its two lows; the higher of the highs is the **higher high water**, the lower of the lows the **lower low water**. On an average day the water rises and falls about 3.5 m (11 feet) between the two, seven times the half metre the bulges allow. It gets the shape wrong: two equal bulges would give two equal highs and two equal lows. And it gets the timing wrong. The tide reaches Seattle as water that has come in from the Pacific, through the Strait and up the Sound, and the Moon overhead is no guide to when high water comes. Even on the open coast the biggest tides come a day or two after new and full moon, as if the ocean were answering late.

Pierre-Simon Laplace saw why in 1775. The ocean cannot heap itself into the equilibrium shape, because the bulges would have to sweep round the Earth faster than water can follow. At the equator they would travel at the Earth's turning speed, about 460 m/s. A wave so long that the ocean is shallow water for it moves at √(g h), lesson 7's rule, and in an ocean 4,000 m deep that is about 200 m/s. The tide is the ocean's answer to the forcing, a set of long waves running round the ocean basins, slowed by their depth and turned by their coasts. Laplace's equations were right, but nobody could solve them for real oceans. Lesson 9 takes the route that worked, measuring the tide and taking it apart into regular waves, and finds the cause of Seattle's unequal tides in the tilt of the Moon's orbit, which carries the Moon north and south of the equator each month. Lesson 10 follows the tide as a wave in a basin, and shows why it grows as it runs up the Sound.

blocks.caption: Six questions on the tide
blocks.task: Choose the best answer to each

items.ask: Why is there a high tide on the side of the Earth facing away from the Moon?
choices: The Moon pulls that water less than the Earth's centre, so it lags behind the Earth's fall toward the Moon
The Moon's gravity passes through the Earth and lifts the water on the far side as well
The Earth's daily spin flings water outward, and most strongly on the side away from the Moon
items.why: The tide comes from the difference between the Moon's pull at a place and its pull at the Earth's centre. The far side is pulled less than the centre, so its water lags behind, away from the centre. The daily spin is the same all round a line of latitude, so it cannot make a bulge that follows the Moon.

items.ask: Why do high tides come about fifty minutes later each day?
choices: The Moon moves on along its orbit, so a place needs 24 h 50 min to come back under it
The Moon's pull weakens through the month, so the water takes a little longer to rise each day
The tide takes a little longer each day to cross the ocean from where it was raised
items.why: While the Earth turns once, the Moon moves about 13 degrees along its orbit, and the Earth must turn a little farther to catch it up. The bulges follow the Moon, so the tides keep the Moon's time.

items.ask: The Sun pulls on the Earth about 180 times harder than the Moon. Why does it raise less than half as much tide?
choices: Its pull barely changes across the Earth's width, because the Sun is so much farther away
Most of its pull goes into holding the Earth in orbit, which leaves little for raising tides
Its tide is raised only by day, on the side of the Earth that is facing the Sun
items.why: A tide comes from the difference in pull across the Earth. For the Sun, 390 times farther than the Moon, the near side is only a 23,000th closer than the centre, so its pull changes by far less: about 0.46 of the Moon's tide.

items.ask: When in the month do spring tides, the biggest ranges, come?
choices: Near new moon and full moon, when the Sun's and Moon's bulges line up
Near full moon only, when the Moon is opposite the Sun and its pull is unopposed
Near the quarter moons, when the Sun and Moon pull at right angles to each other
items.why: Each pair of bulges points along a line through the Earth. At new moon and at full moon the Sun, Earth and Moon are in a line, so either way the bulges line up and add.

items.ask: At the first quarter moon, what does the Sun do to the Moon's tide?
choices: Its bulges sit where the Moon's lows are, so the highs are lower and the lows higher
It pulls against the Moon and cancels its tide completely for a day or two
It adds its bulges on top of the Moon's, just as it does at full moon
items.why: At the quarters the Sun is at right angles to the Moon. Its bulges fill in the Moon's lows, and the range falls to about 0.54 of the Moon's own: smaller, but not gone, because the Sun's tide is under half the Moon's.

items.ask: The equilibrium tide has a range of about half a metre, but Seattle's average daily range is about 3.5 m. What explains most of the difference?
choices: The ocean answers the forcing as long waves in basins, which can grow far larger than the bulges
Seattle lies closer to the Moon's path than most places, so the Moon pulls harder on its water
The Sound's water is fresher and lighter than seawater, so the same pull lifts it higher
items.why: The bulges cannot keep up with the turning Earth, so the tide travels as long waves round the ocean and up the Sound, and their size and timing are set by the basins: the subject of lessons 9 and 10.

centrifugal.title: The centrifugal explanation
centrifugal.text: Many books explain the far bulge by the Earth and Moon swinging round their shared balance point, which flings the far side's water outward. Done carefully it gives the same answer as the difference in pull, because that swing is the same fall toward the Moon described here, shared by every point of the Earth. Done carelessly it suggests the Earth's daily spin matters, which it does not: the spin is the same all round each line of latitude, so it cannot make a bulge that follows the Moon.

tractive.title: Where the push is strongest
tractive.text: Directly under the Moon and directly opposite it, the tide-raising force points straight up and has no sideways part. Halfway round, it points straight down. The sideways part is strongest in between, about 45 degrees from the point under the Moon, and it always pushes the water toward the nearer of the two bulges.

cube.title: Why the cube
cube.text: A pull that falls as one over the distance squared, 1/d², changes across a small width a by about 2a/d of itself. The pull is mass/d², so the difference goes as (mass/d²) × (2a/d), or 2 × mass × a / d³: the cube of distance. The Sun is about 27 million times as massive as the Moon and 390 times as far, and 390³ is about 59 million, so its tide is about 27/59, or 0.46, of the Moon's.

spring.title: Spring
spring.text: Spring tides have nothing to do with the season. The word is the old sense of spring as a leap or rising, as in a spring of water, and spring tides come every two weeks all year round. Neap is an old word for the low tides between them; where it comes from is unknown.

perigee.title: The Moon's distance
perigee.text: The Moon's orbit is not a circle. Its distance varies from about 363,000 km at its nearest (perigee) to about 406,000 km at its farthest (apogee), and since the tide-raising force goes with the cube of distance, it is about 40% stronger at perigee than at apogee. A spring tide near perigee is one ingredient of the king tides, the year's highest tides, which lesson 10 takes up.
